# Independent audit: weak added laws at an ordinary simplex


ordinary-simplex-depth-first-variation-under-weak-added-laws.md.
The exact verifier supporting computation verify_ordinary_simplex_depth_first_variation.py
reran successfully: 88 checks. No correction is required.

## Attainment and localization

For a fixed normal, the closed-cap mass is upper semicontinuous in
the candidate point even when the added measure has atoms. Its
infimum over normals is upper semicontinuous. On the compact simplex
it therefore attains its maximum. Every point outside the simplex
interior has a separating or supporting cap of zero simplex volume,
so its perturbed depth is at most t. Since the centroid has depth
at least Gamma V, all global maximizers are interior when t<Gamma V.
No compact-support assumption on the approximating measures is needed
for this argument.

Every canonical cap has added mass at most t. The explicit cap
formula V(1-lambda_i(y))^d consequently bounds each barycentric
coordinate above by 1/m+eta_t. Their sum gives the complementary
lower bounds and hence a uniform O(t) displacement for every
maximizer. The printed derivative bound for eta_t has the correct
power and volume factor. This is a rate obtained from the simplex
geometry, not from weak convergence.

## Moving caps and the all-normal lower bound

The moving-halfspace convergence statement is valid. Tightness
controls the mass outside a fixed large ball. On that ball the
moving affine forms converge uniformly. Fixed shifted open/closed
halflines sandwich the moving caps, and the null mass of the limiting
canonical hyperplane removes the final boundary ambiguity. This
allows arbitrary atoms in nu_t and requires no rate for nu_t -> nu.

The only equality normals of the unperturbed simplex at its centroid
are the canonical apex-side directions. This follows from the
previously audited ordinary Grunbaum equality characterization:
an equality pyramid representation of a simplex must use one vertex
as apex and its opposite facet as base. The interval case has its
two ordinary directions.

Near such a direction all vertex margins retain their strict
one-positive, d-negative sign pattern. The rational cap formula
therefore supplies genuine smoothness and a uniform point derivative.
In the lower-bound contradiction, a limiting approximately minimizing
normal must be canonical. The source correctly retains
F(g,u_t)-Gamma V >= 0 rather than imposing any unproved convergence
rate on u_t. The remaining uniform Taylor term and moving added-cap
mass give the stated coefficient p_i-kappa l_i(v_*).

Thus the lower bound is over all normals. No atomic cap-infimum
attainment or finite-direction sufficiency is assumed.

## Matching upper bound and all maximizers

The canonical upper bounds at an arbitrary maximizer have an O(t^2)
simplex remainder and a t o(1) added-law remainder. Their average
cancels the barycentric displacement exactly, proving the matching
coefficient pbar. Subtracting the attained value from each canonical
upper bound gives m asymptotically nonnegative quantities whose
sum is exactly zero. Each consequently tends to zero. Injectivity of
the barycentric linear map proves the displacement formula for
every maximizing selection, including nonunique finite-t maxima.

## Thin-cone application and its interior conclusion

The thin vertex matrix is epsilon I+g 1^T, with determinant
epsilon^(d-1)(h+epsilon). Its uniform laws converge to the stated
Beta(d,1) radial law on [0,g]. The limiting canonical masses are
(1,0,...,0), with zero boundary masses. Division by N gives precisely
t=|E_epsilon|/N; restoring mass yields the coefficients in (18)-(19).

For the stronger geometric conclusion, the inverse matrix has norm
O(1/epsilon), while the common error is o(e_epsilon). Their product
is o(1) for d>=2 because e_epsilon/epsilon stays bounded. The
non-apex barycentrics thus tend to 1/d. Their sum has positive
remaining apex weight
[epsilon+d theta-sum r_i]/(epsilon+h), since theta is a fixed
positive multiple of e_epsilon and sum r_i=o(e_epsilon).
All maximizing points are therefore inside the thin simplex.
The uniformity over maximizers follows by the stated sequential
contradiction. The exclusion of d=1 for this thin-law application
is necessary and is present.

The null-boundary counterexample has the asserted two different
derivatives for the same weak limit. It correctly identifies a
substantive hypothesis rather than a proof convenience.

The conclusion remains an ordinary projected-measure theorem.
Neither the proof nor this audit promotes it to an oblique
mixed-depth lower bound.
